item.title: Federal government holds American Samoa seabed mineral lease sale despite judge's ruling
item.description: The Marine Minerals Administration held a lease sale for offshore critical minerals near American Samoa, despite a federal judge’s ruling days earlier voiding the government’s environmental assessment. The administration said two areas covering 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa were leased for $6 million.
item.content:encoded:
The Marine Minerals Administration held a lease sale for offshore critical minerals near American Samoa, despite a federal judge’s ruling days earlier voiding the government’s environmental assessment.

The administration said two areas covering 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa were leased for $6 million.

Earthjustice, the environmental law firm that sued the federal government in the U.S. District Court of Hawaii, says it will pursue legal action to stop the leases.

“In deciding to move forward with today’s sale, the Trump administration has performed a renegade, unlawful act — a gambit that drew a single bidder offering the minimum price for the leases,” Earthjustice Ocean’s attorney Chris Eaton said in a news release. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided. Deep-sea mining will cause unprecedented destruction to some of the ocean’s most pristine and unexplored reaches, and we will continue to fight for their protection.”

The case is being closely watched in the Marianas, where up to 69 million acres of seabed along both sides of the island chain are set to be leased on Dec. 16.

Last year, President Donald Trump ordered government agencies to fast-track seabed mineral exploration and extraction. He said critical minerals contained in polymetallic nodules found on the ocean floor are essential to U.S. economic and national security interests.

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the lease sale is delivering on Trump’s order.

“Critical minerals are used in everything from electronics to defense systems. A dependable critical minerals supply chain is essential to American manufacturing and the technologies that power our economy and national defense,” Burgum said. “Today’s sale opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply."

item.title: Sen. Christopher Dueñas selected as next legislative speaker
item.description: The Republican Party of Guam announced that Sen. Christopher Dueñas has been selected as the speaker of the 39 th Guam Legislature. Dueñas will continue to oversee the Office of Finance and Budget.
item.content:encoded:
The Republican Party of Guam announced that Sen. Christopher Dueñas has been selected as the speaker of the 39 th Guam Legislature.

Dueñas will continue to oversee the Office of Finance and Budget.

He said he looks forward to working with lawmakers from both parties to build a stronger, more prosperous Guam.

“Through the Office of Finance and Budget, I remain committed to responsible budgeting, fiscal discipline, and finally realizing the full implementation of performance-based budgeting, ensuring that government expenditures translate into measurable results for our people,” Dueñas said.

Sen. Telo Taitague will be vice speaker, and Shelly Calvo will be the legislative secretary.

Sen. Jesse Lujan will serve as majority leader, and Vincent Borja will be the majority whip.

Sen. Sabrina Salas-Matanane will chair the Committee on Rules.

The party said remaining committee chair assignments will be announced soon.

item.title: USS Frank Cable visits Saipan
item.description: The submarine tender USS Frank Cable visited Saipan over the weekend as part of an effort between CNMI leadership and Joint Region Marianas to bring more Navy ship visits to Saipan. Rear Adm. Brett Mietus said the people of the Northern Marianas have always welcomed Navy sailors like family, and the visit are good for the local economy.
item.content:encoded:
The submarine tender USS Frank Cable visited Saipan over the weekend as part of an effort between CNMI leadership and Joint Region Marianas to bring more Navy ship visits to Saipan.

Rear Adm. Brett Mietus said the people of the Northern Marianas have always welcomed Navy sailors like family, and the visit are good for the local economy.

“This visit is the result of listening to Commonwealth leaders and working together to make a great port visit,” Mietus said.

Port visits give sailors the chance to experience the culture of the CNMI, while bringing crew members into local restaurants, shops and attractions.

“We value our partnership with the CNMI, and we look forward to continuing our work so more of our ships and sailors can experience the commonwealth’s hospitality.”

During the visit Frank Cable sailors were scheduled to visit Gregorio T. Camacho Elementary School to assist with campus cleanup and beautification.

The visit reflects continued collaboration between the military and the Office of the Governor, Commonwealth Bureau of Military Affairs, Marianas Visitors Authority and Saipan Chamber of Commerce.

item.content:encoded:
ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate change talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels. On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.

The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions .

After the EU walked out, so did other countries pushing for a speedy transition away from fossil fuels.

The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."

This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.

Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts , like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035 . That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.

"It's good that that decision has been rejected," says Mohamed Adow, of Power Shift Africa, a nonprofit focused on climate change in Africa. "It doesn't have enough to help protect the people who are most vulnerable to climate change, who have contributed the least and are now suffering firsthand the worst."

NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits .

item.title: Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment
item.description: Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people . The coverage choices are complex and often consequential. Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.
item.content:encoded:
Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people . The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.

Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.

Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn't one plan. It's more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.

Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there's no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn't cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.

As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D , the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.

This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.

"People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs," said David Lipschutz , a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It's a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can't find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn't tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.

Some beneficiaries who didn't have to pay monthly premiums in recent years will begin paying for prescription drug Part D coverage in 2027. While that change follows the 2025 introduction of federal caps on out-of-pocket drug expenses, it comes as the Trump administration is ending temporary federal subsidies that helped keep premiums down. The cap on out-of-pocket expenses for prescription drugs in 2027 will be $2,400, a total enrollees can opt to spread out over the course of the year.

Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said people who don't shop around could be leaving money on the table.

"It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027," she said.

An estimated 4.3 million people now have to look for a new Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan after private insurers left the market. Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they'll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it's important to read the fine print and add up the other costs.

"There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage plans provide," Lipschutz said.

So ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover?

And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage plans, Cubanski said, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027.

"Look at that dollar value specifically," she said.

For those moving to traditional Medicare, it won't come with a drug plan, so enrollees must sign up for a new Part D plan if they want most prescriptions covered. Enrollees who miss that step when they are first eligible may not have drug coverage for the coming year, and they may face a late-enrollment penalty on their monthly premiums for life.

When selecting a drug plan, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don't pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage.

If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap plan, with no health screening. After that, all bets are off: Insurers in most states can turn enrollees down or charge more because of a health condition. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, and New York are exceptions .

Enrollees whose Advantage plans have not been renewed — and haven't been consolidated into another plan — can switch to traditional Medicare and buy a Medigap policy without a health screening, but they need to act before March.

Medicare experts advise enrollees to write down all their prescription drugs, as well as any procedures planned in the next year, such as a joint replacement or dental work, to help them decide which plan will cover their needs. Call a favorite doctor's office to see whether they are in-network for the plans being considered. Remember that brokers might earn commissions, especially on Advantage plans, and might not represent every plan.

For unbiased help, every state has a federally funded State Health Insurance Assistance Program that offers free plan counseling specific to your situation, in person and over the phone. To get help, go to the website at shiphelp.org/open-enrollment , email info@shiphelp.org, or call the SHIP National Technical Assistance Center at 877-839-2675.

A SHIP counselor can also help enrollees apply for benefits that help pay for Medicare premiums and prescription drug costs, such as the Medicare Savings Programs and Medicare Part D Extra Help .

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

item.title: NPR's Senior Podcast Challenge: Early entries we love
item.description: Once people hit retirement age, there are so many questions: Who am I without my job? What do I do to fill this time? How are my relationships changing? This fall, for the first-ever NPR Senior Podcast Challenge , we asked those of you in the over-65 crowd, to tell us about all this, and you've been sending in your answers.
item.content:encoded:
Once people hit retirement age, there are so many questions: Who am I without my job? What do I do to fill this time? How are my relationships changing?

This fall, for the first-ever NPR Senior Podcast Challenge , we asked those of you in the over-65 crowd, to tell us about all this, and you've been sending in your answers.

The competition flips the story line on our popular NPR Student Podcast Challenge – since 2018 more than 90,000 young people have sent us their stories , in their own voices .

Now, we're hearing from listeners with a lot of experience, hopefully some wisdom, and perhaps more grey hair.

While the contest is still open for a few more weeks — you have until November 30 to enter — we've been listening to more than 100 podcasts that have come in so far.

Here's a sample of some of our early favorites:

Lou Ann Baylock, of Sarasota, Fla., told us she wasn't too happy about the title of our contest: the "senior" part.

"I'm 68, but I'm NOT a senior, am I?" she asks in her podcast, Talk to Me .

"I thought seniors were people in their 80s," she says. "I mean, I see my body changing. I know I'm getting older. But am I really a senior?"

Baylock ends up deciding she's OK with that term: She's still working, and as a therapist she tells us in her podcast she has some ideas that might help other people her age.

Many of our podcasters took up the issue of life after retirement. Some of you are telling us you're having the best time of your life. Others, not so much.

For Martin Goldsmith, 78, of Tacoma, Wash., retirement means not letting his age keep him doing the things he loves.

"The back, the legs, and the joints aren't what they used to be," he says in his entry Joy Filled Retirement . "So for me, the running and skiing are out and the hearing aids are in."

But, he adds, "I can still play my guitar."

Music, Goldsmith tells us, has always been in his DNA. He grew up jamming with his dad on the clarinet and mom on the viola. And he's now playing his guitar at the children's hospital, and he ends his story playing and singing an old favorite, Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out .

And then, there's dating. We've received quite a few podcasts about life post-divorce, or after losing a partner.

Our podcasters are reminding us that it never gets easier, and many of them including George Smith have told us some version of this: "I never thought I'd be here."

Smith lives with his daughter in Wildomar, Calif., and when it came to figuring out the modern dating scene, he says:

"After almost three decades of marriage, I found myself in my mid-60s, divorced, alone in a cafe, and about to meet a woman from a dating app for the first time in my life. Little did I realize," he tells us, "my teenage daughter Shannon would become my dating navigator."

Smith's podcast is aptly called Swipe Right, Dad , and he tells us about three very different online dates he goes on.

Our competition, will close on Nov. 30. You can submit here .

Podcasts submitted must be completely original work, no longer than eight minutes in length . We encourage stories of all kinds – from personal narratives to in-depth interviews to fully reported audio journalism.

Some key rules: No copyrighted music. And, this should come as no surprise: keep AI out of your writing and presentation.

See the rules page for exact requirements and restrictions.

You can submit multiple podcasts. Please fill out a separate form for each entry.

We'll choose several finalists and our grand-prize winner early in the new year and air the winning podcast on Weekend Edition Sunday in January or February.

If you have no idea where to get started, don't worry! You don't need to be an audio expert, and you can make a podcast with nothing more than a smart phone, a computer, and some easily available editing software. You can check out our student podcasting resources page , which includes step-by-step instructions, from choosing a good story, conducting interviews, writing a script, and tips for editing and mixing. And you can subscribe to our newsletter for the latest from the contest team.

And finally, if you have questions about the Senior Podcast Challenge, email us at seniorpodcastchallenge@npr.org .

item.title: He expected a small-business loan. He got a 7-year nightmare
item.description: GLENDALE, Calif. — Sitting at his desk, tucked into a corner of his teenage bedroom — a place where he'd never intended to return, well into middle age — Vahe Shahinian rereads the emails that split his life into before and after. A broker was offering to fund Shahinian's small business with a line of credit worth $750,000.
item.content:encoded:
GLENDALE, Calif. — Sitting at his desk, tucked into a corner of his teenage bedroom — a place where he'd never intended to return, well into middle age — Vahe Shahinian rereads the emails that split his life into before and after.

A broker was offering to fund Shahinian's small business with a line of credit worth $750,000.

It was 2019, and Shahinian's company soared, like a miniature Live Nation-Ticketmaster, selling tickets and producing concerts around Los Angeles and beyond. He imagined how much he could do with stable funding .

The pitch had a catch: Shahinian would first accept a third of the sum and start paying it back immediately, in daily installments of $3,600. After 30 days, he could access the rest of the money. He crunched the numbers, followed up with questions — and took the deal.

Shahinian sent the daily payments, he says, for 30 days. Then 40. Then 50.

"From that day," he says, "it's been one long day, one long nightmare."

For seven years, Shahinian has been mired in the shadowy industry that is now the fastest-growing source of funding for small business in the United States. It's largely unregulated, promising fast money at a tremendous cost. And Shahinian's lawsuit against his funders could become one of the first of its kind to go to trial.

Before the "incident," as Shahinian calls his fateful deal, he'd been in business for 15 years, building his company from a side hustle into his main source of income.

Educated as a computer scientist, he'd spent years programming satellites as an aerospace engineer. In 2004, he also developed a site for something he loved in his spare time: community events. Shahinian called his platform for ticketing and seating charts It's My Seat.

Over a decade, Shahinian grew his business from selling tickets to galas and festivals to producing his own shows: booking artists and venues, promoting and marketing. His first concert, by a flamenco guitarist, sold 400 seats. The next, 700. Three years later, 1960s crooner Engelbert Humperdinck performed for 3,000. In 2015, Shahinian expanded again, into touring.

Like most U.S. small businesses, Shahinian says, he self-funded for years. Entrepreneurs like him often dip into savings, family money or home equity; many run up credit cards and reinvest profits.

Shahinian says he had qualified for several generous credit cards, including an American Express with essentially no spending limit. Later, Amex also repeatedly approved him for special merchant financing: instant short-term loans with a low interest rate of 6%.

"All my life," Shahinian offers as his frequent disclaimer these days, "I had never had one missed payment."

By 2018, Shahinian says, he had built his retirement plan: His ticket sales climbed toward $5 million a year, his profits $250,000.

Booking his biggest tour yet, with a 1980s German superstar, Shahinian sought his fifth round of Amex merchant funding.

Except this time, Amex said no. The company was phasing out the program.

All Shahinian could think was: "Whoa." Tours are costly affairs with down payments to venues, marketing, airfare, lights and sound. He'd left himself no time to maneuver — two weeks to acquire about $200,000.

Small businesses in the U.S. consistently say they turn to merchant cash advances, MCAs, because they find few alternatives, especially in an emergency.

Most traditional lending takes months and vigorous vetting. The Small Business Administration has tightened its lending rules . Big banks reject about 20% of business loan applications, according to the Treasury Department , and respond to a quarter with only partial funding. A recent Federal Reserve survey found even lower odds.

MCAs, by contrast, present themselves as a lifeline, offering large sums within hours.

Their fees, however, run from 25% to 200% and more, when translated into an annual rate. MCA firms argue they charge a lot because they take on big risks.

They also face almost no regulatory oversight.

MCAs escape most lending laws because, technically, they are not loans. An MCA is meant to be a purchase of future sales — a business gets cash in exchange for a steady cut of its earnings later. MCA funders generally aren't required to be licensed and face no legal limit to how much they can charge.

The industry runs the gamut: A funder could be a firm recommended by Amazon, or the latest fintech startup, or a former subprime mortgage lender. Some rely on brokers to drum up deals. Most collect payment by withdrawing directly from their borrowers' bank accounts — often daily.

Shahinian, scrambling after the Amex rejection, lined up two cash advances for a total of $250,000, he says, owing back almost $400,000. This saved his concert tour but cost him all the profits.

"It was my fault — I waited last minute," Shahinian says. "I'm talking to myself, 'Vahe, you had to do it this time. You're never going back to MCAs.'"

But MCA pitches never stop . Sometimes, Shahinian replied that he wanted only a traditional loan, something along an 8% interest rate.

Before he even went hunting, the offer came to him — the pitch that changed his life: The line of credit up to $750,000 at an annual interest rate just under 9%. Finally, Shahinian thought, someone recognized the quality of his business.

"It's like the puzzle fit, you know?" he says.

This encounter took Shahinian beyond the MCAs' unforgiving fees into what he alleges was fraud.
